name: Aaron Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior electrician with a commercial fit-out firm, about forty people, and we kit out offices, mostly, plus the odd shop or restaurant. Right now I'm on the fourth floor of an insurance building putting in floor boxes and lighting grids, running containment all day off a scissor lift. I start at seven, the site's loud, and my foreman Dele gives me the drawings and checks my terminations. I'm still slow on the fire alarm side, I'll admit that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Big site, lots of trades, everyone taking the mick at break. What grinds me down is the rework, when the designer changes the layout for the fifth time and we pull out a day's cable. The pay's good though, better than most juniors get, and my partner Lena and I have about eight months saved plus a bit in an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get back to talking about pay and housing. At work it'd be a non-story, the lads would joke about the robot that never showed up. Online I'd maybe share a post about how the money should have gone into public services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Offices keep getting refitted every few years, so my firm's order book stays full. A world where offices keep getting refitted every five years is a world where I always have work. The only thing that'd bother me is that rent is mad, and Lena and I still can't buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, get my fire alarm module done by spring, and finish my licence. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then to look up regs, like I do. And I'd keep putting 600 a month toward a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit bored by it, even. It's the version where the only fight is the usual one, about wages and houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent is mad. Is that a worry for you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. Lena's a nurse on nights and we pay nearly a third of what we earn on a one-bed. But we've got a cushion and I'm getting a pay rise once I'm licensed, so it's an annoyance more than a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using a chatbot for the regs. How much do you actually rely on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not loads. I'll check something like cable sizes for a long run, then ask Dele anyway, because I don't fully trust it. It's handy for the boring lookups, but I wouldn't let it tell me how to wire a distribution board.

say: I'd say **good**, now let's talk about pay and housing again.
At work it'd be a **non-story**, a joke about the robot that never came.
think: My firm's **order book** stays full because offices keep getting refitted.
The real pressure is **rent**, which still keeps us from buying.
do: Finish the **fire alarm module** by spring and then my licence.
Keep using the chatbot **now and then** for regs lookups.
Keep putting **600 a month** toward a house deposit.
S0.quote: A world where offices keep getting refitted every five years is a world where I always have work.
fieldNote: His job security depends on **office refits**, which a flat AI world protects.
Uses AI as a **lookup tool** but double-checks with his foreman.
Housing, not technology, is his **daily pressure**.

steps.text: Finish the fire alarm module by spring
Put 600 a month toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we're fine, they can't send a chatbot up a scissor lift. To friends I'd say the government needs to make companies share the gains, through shorter hours or better pay. I'd probably share a union post about retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a bit worried, but not about the tools. It's that our customers are offices. If insurance firms need fewer staff, they need fewer floors, and fewer floors means fewer fit-outs. My job isn't threatened by robots, it's threatened by insurance companies needing half the desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start picking up domestic and shop work on the side, weekends with a mate, so I'm not only an office guy. I'd use the AI planning tools the firm brings in, once the older lads show it works. I'd keep saving for the deposit but maybe hold it in cash longer rather than buy straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked. My hands are still needed, but I can see the work changing shape around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the site do you think feels this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimators and the CAD drawing team in our office, for sure. My mate Callum does the drawings, and he's already said the software can lay out a floor in an hour. I'd feel for him, he's got a kid on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the older lads to prove the tools work. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen too many shiny apps get dumped after six months. I'll pick it up once it's actually saving someone time. That's just how I am, I don't like being the guinea pig, but I don't like being last either.

say: I'd say they **can't send** a chatbot up a scissor lift.
I'd say companies should **share the gains** through shorter hours or better pay.
think: The threat is **fewer office floors**, not robots, since our clients are offices.
Fewer staff means **fewer fit-outs** for my firm.
do: Pick up **domestic and shop** work at weekends with a mate.
Use the firm's **AI planning tools** once others prove them.
Hold the deposit in **cash** for longer before buying.
feel: **Sorry** for colleagues in drawing and estimating.
S1.quote: My job isn't threatened by robots, it's threatened by insurance companies needing half the desks.
fieldNote: He spots a **second-order** risk: fewer office workers means fewer office fit-outs.
Classic steady adopter, waits for **proof** before using new tools.
Diversifying into **domestic work** is his hedge.

steps.text: Do weekend shop and house jobs with a mate
Use the firm's AI planning tools once others trust them
Keep the house deposit in cash for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a crisis and the government should tax the AI firms and pay people through it. At work I'd push for the union to get a deal on redundancy. Online I'd be one of those people sharing everything, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my firm could fold. If the thinking AI arrives in 2028, office work collapses first, and nobody refits an office that's half empty. Then the robots come around 2031 for the rest of us. My firm fits out offices, so when the office workers go, my firm goes about a year later. That keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd move to a domestic firm, or a firm that does hospitals and schools, places that still need people. I'd get my licence and the EV charger ticket inside the year. We'd shelve buying the flat and keep the deposit as our safety net. I'd join the union properly, not just pay subs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's dropping. I'm 27 and everything I'd planned, the flat, the licence, a kid one day, would feel shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about the night this became real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we have a kid at all, honestly. Lena's job would probably be safer than mine, nurses are hands-on and caring. I'd say let's hold off, and she'd say we always hold off. That conversation would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the robots coming three years after the thinking AI, what's the plan for those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze every bit of work out of them. Hospitals, schools, care homes, old housing, places with awkward wiring. Save everything I can, maybe 1,200 a month if we skip holidays. And hope the government's sorted something by 2031, though I wouldn't bet on it.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** and demand taxes on AI firms to fund support.
At work I'd push the union for a **redundancy deal**.
think: My firm could **fold**, because nobody refits an empty office.
Robots around **2031** would then come for the rest of my work.
do: Move to a firm doing **hospitals and schools** this year.
Get my licence and an **EV charger** ticket inside the year.
Shelve the **flat purchase** and keep the deposit as a safety net.
feel: **Shaky** about the flat, the licence and having a child.
S2.quote: My firm fits out offices, so when the office workers go, my firm goes about a year later.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his current job** within about a year of 2028, so this is alarm, not unease.
His **savings** and plenty of local jobs give him moves, but the plans feel shaky.
The **family decision** about a child is where the fear really lands.

steps.text: Apply to an electrical firm doing hospitals and schools
Take the EV charger installation course this year
Shelve the flat purchase and keep the deposit
Join the union as an active member

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it to anyone: five years is enough to get ready if the government starts now. I'd push for a national retraining scheme. At work I'd say the firm should get out of offices and into public buildings while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think it's still bad for my firm, just slower. Offices thin out by 2031, robots arrive about 2034, when I'm 35. I could ride the office work for three or four years, then move. Five years gives me time to jump ship before the office work dries up, instead of after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay with the firm two or three years, get the licence and the inspection qualification. Then move to public sector maintenance, schools or the council. Keep saving 800 a month. Maybe buy the flat after all, since we'd have time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd still feel it, but it'd be the kind of worry that makes you do things, not the kind that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to bring your crew with you when you jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them, for sure. Dele's 55, he'd probably retire. The younger lads, I'd push them to get the inspection ticket too. I'm not the type to sneak off without telling anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat in this one but not the fast one. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to change jobs before it bites. In the fast one, I'd be buying just as my income might drop. With five years I'd have a new job sorted before the robots and still have time to pay a chunk off.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to prepare** if the government starts now.
I'd tell the firm to shift into **public buildings** while there's time.
think: It's still bad for my firm, just **slower**.
I'd have time to **jump ship** before the office work dries up.
do: Stay two or three years and get the **inspection qualification**.
Move to **council or school** maintenance before 2031.
Save **800 a month** and maybe still buy the flat.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind of worry that makes you act.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to jump ship before the office work dries up, instead of after.
fieldNote: He still expects his **current job** to go, but now has control over timing.
**Timing** of the house purchase is directly tied to warning time.
Wants to **bring colleagues** along, consistent with his progressive outlook.

steps.text: Take the inspection and testing qualification within three years
Move to council or school maintenance before 2031
Save 800 a month and buy the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it properly: free training, shorter weeks, unions at the table. At work, I'd be the guy telling everyone it's coming but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm all right. By the time robots come, around 2039, I'd be 40, licensed, maybe a supervisor. A decade is long enough for me to become the man who checks the robots' work. My bigger worry would be the people who never get warned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the licence, inspection ticket, then go for supervisor in five years. Learn the AI design and testing tools as they come in, once they're proven. Buy the flat next year. Keep the index fund ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not much more. It feels like a long road with a corner at the end that I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check the robots' work. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Testing and certifying, mostly. Someone's still got to put their name on a certificate saying the building won't burn down. I'd want to be that person, and that means being properly good at testing, which right now I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Callum, who does the drawings, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get out of drawings now, mate, while you can still pick your next thing. Ten years sounds long, but the design software would get there way before the robots. My friend Callum's the one who'd need the decade more than me.

say: I'd say a decade means **free training**, shorter weeks and unions at the table.
At work I'd say it's coming but **there's time**.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40, licensed and maybe a supervisor.
My bigger worry is the people who **never get warned**.
do: Aim for **supervisor** within five years after the inspection ticket.
Learn AI **design and testing** tools once they're proven.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a corner he can see coming.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough for me to become the man who checks the robots' work.
fieldNote: The decade lets him picture himself **certifying** the robots' work.
His concern shifts to **others**, especially office-side colleagues.
Still **steady**: adopts tools once proven, not first.

steps.text: Work toward a supervisor role within five years
Learn the firm's AI design and testing tools
Buy the flat with Lena next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my firm lives off offices and offices would empty first. What'd help is a real retraining fund paid for by AI companies, and a union deal so firms can't just drop people. Nobody refits an empty office, and that's the bit of AI nobody on my site has thought about yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about housing. Every picture you described, I kept thinking about whether we could still buy a flat. For people my age that's tied up with all of it.

headlineQuote: Nobody refits an empty office, and that's the bit of AI nobody on my site has thought about yet.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old junior** on commercial office fit-outs, with eight months saved and an index fund.
His fear isn't robots but **emptying offices**, since his firm depends on office refits.
He adopts tools **once proven** and hedges by moving toward public buildings.
Calm in AI Plateau, he becomes **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and steadies with more warning time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because office work would collapse and his **firm could fold**.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid for by AI companies.
A **union deal** stopping firms from dropping people overnight.
